chapter_theme: Civakan's friends reach the outskirts of Emamapuram and plan to raid the king's herd to draw him into battle, until Buddhisenan warns of the blame of retreat and the cost of blood; their three spies then report how Civakan tamed the king's must elephant Valaya Sundaram, rode it before the king, and was acclaimed as the one master of elephants.
structure_note: 1820-1823 the journey and the grove; 1824-1829 council (Padumukan proposes, Buddhisenan objects); 1830-1842 the spies' report of the elephant's taming.

1820.reading: Swimming the broad rivers ringed by flowering groves, past tall golden hills where honey hung on the sandal trees, split by the moon's horn, falls in streams of nectar, the company reached a land thick with people.
1820.event: Civakan's companions and their force cross hills and rivers and reach a populous country.
1820.nuance: The verb சென்றது has no named subject; the next verses show it is the band of Civakan's friends travelling in search of him.

1821.reading: Those who were like poison-fanged snakes came to a river bank four kaatham from the city whose white mansions rise like the foam of milk boiling over in new pots.
1821.event: The companions halt on a river bank four kaatham from Emamapuram.
1821.nuance: The companions are named only by a simile of menace, poison-fanged snakes, which prepares the plan of attack that follows.

1822.reading: The four, with their force, came without delay to the white-sand bank of a forest river, a grove of honey where sunlight could not pierce, its curve like the waist of doe-eyed women.
1822.event: The four friends reach a shaded grove on the river bank.

1823.reading: Honey dripping, toddy breathing, flowers spread over the long sand and bees crowding the clustered blossoms above, the grove they entered had a nature hard to leave once one had come in.

1824.reading: Seated in the rich shade, Padumukan, out of love, asks the others to say how they may reach the peerless-chested man with the honeyed garland.
1824.event: Padumukan asks his fellows how they may reach Civakan.

1825.reading: Padumukan proposes that once they have seized the bright herds of the glorious king's city, they will meet the mighty one face to face on the field, and no harm will come of it.
1825.event: Padumukan proposes raiding the king's herds to draw Civakan out to battle.
1825.nuance: The raid is a lure: the friends count on Civakan riding out against cattle raiders as he did for the herdsmen of Rajamapuram, and on recognising him in the fight.

1826.reading: After they have traded bows, he says, if the fight comes to swords they can quickly bring him back, so rise eager; so the garlanded one told all his men.
1826.event: Padumukan rouses his men for the raid.
1826.nuance: மீட்கலாம் may mean that they can win Civakan back or that they can pull out of the fight; the sense of the plan turns on which.

1827.reading: Buddhisenan objects that if, after they take the herd, the lord is not in the guarded city and the great army comes out, turning back will bring blame, and he has more to say.
1827.event: Buddhisenan warns that the raid may bring the king's army and not Civakan.

claims.claim: to withdraw from a fight once begun brings blame

1827.nuance: The objection exposes the flaw in the lure: the plan depends on Civakan being in the city, which no one has checked.

1828.reading: Like lightning flashing in a cloud-filled sky, the swords of honest warriors will flash and elephants will plunge in a flood of leaping blood, so, men of unfailing resolve, think and decide.

claims.claim: a battle, once joined, becomes a flood of blood, so it must be weighed before it is begun

1829.reading: So spoke Buddhisenan of the four Vedas; as the four sat, agreeing that this was the point, the three spies they had sent ahead came together and announced what had happened that day.
1829.event: The friends accept Buddhisenan's counsel, and their three spies return with news.
1829.nuance: நான்மறையினான் makes Buddhisenan a man of the four Vedas, a Brahmin counsellor among the friends. The three spies who come in agreement (ஒன்றி) recall the Kural's rule that three spies' concurring word is to be trusted, though ஒன்றி may instead go with the sending.

1830.reading: The spies tell of Valaya Sundaram, the king's elephant like a great mountain of collyrium, with pearl-filled tusks like the young crescent, the lord of five hundred young cow-elephants.
1830.nuance: From here to 1842 the account follows the spies' announcement (இயம்புகின்றார்கள், 1829), and 1838's என்பவே and 1842's என்மரும் keep the voice of report; the passage may also be read as the poet's own narration. Line 3 to 4 (கேழரக் களைய) divides doubtfully.

1831.reading: Raging in its fierce must and roaring like a rain cloud, it killed the mahouts who could not let it go, broke from its post and the cow-elephant, burst its bonds and at that hour went wild.
1831.event: The king's elephant goes into must, kills its mahouts and breaks loose.

1832.reading: Civakan subdued the noble elephant, whose skin seemed scorched by the fire its eyes spat and over which singing bees swarmed, and it grew meek as the minds of women in jewelled girdles.
1832.nuance: The simile likens the tamed beast to the hearts of women won by the hero, the epic's recurring picture of Civakan as one who masters both.

1833.reading: Like a lion with shining teeth climbing a steep hill, the broad-chested man seized the rope and swiftly mounted the rare elephant, and the great crowd roared like the sea's waves.
1833.event: Civakan mounts the elephant and the crowd roars.

1834.reading: As the garlanded youth patted it with his palm, calling it fondly, the great elephant, swelling with joy, did with its trunk the trained responses it knew.
1834.event: Civakan calms the elephant with pats and it answers to his commands.
1834.nuance: அப்புதா தையென is read here as fond calls to the beast (அப்பு, தாதை); the word division is doubtful.

1835.reading: He bound the neck rope doubled with its tassel knot, set the goad in his strong hand, tied on the two bells together and fastened the shining gold forehead plate, like lightning on a snowy hill.
1835.event: Civakan harnesses the elephant with rope, goad, bells and forehead plate.

1836.reading: He girded its belt, hung on the two sounding bells, set both his feet in the rope at its head and neck, and showed such strength that even the king above longed to see him.
1836.event: Civakan finishes the harness and sits ready, admired by the king.

1837.reading: When the victorious king, standing within the walled women's quarter, said 'let us see the lord's riding; bring it here', Civakan drove the elephant in like wind, like the sea, like thunder on a black hill, like Death.
1837.event: At the king's bidding Civakan rides the elephant into the palace court.
1837.nuance: The king is not named; he is presumably Tadamittan of Emamapuram, Civakan's host. கோற்றொடிப் புரிசை, the enclosure of the bangled women, puts the display before the palace women, among them Kanakamalai.

1838.reading: They say he sat beyond any painter's power, like a young god flying lightly with a hill in his grasp, or a god riding a rain cloud.
1838.nuance: Who the young god carrying a hill is (குழவியஞ் செல்வன்) is not clear from the verse; the image fits the hero high on the mountain-like beast.

1839.reading: Like a potter's spinning wheel, or the wheel of time that runs over living beings with swift horses, he made it trace in a twinkling the circles, the straight courses and the rows that the art requires.
1839.event: Civakan puts the elephant through its circling and straight gaits.
1839.nuance: The second simile is காலசக்கரம், the wheel of time that passes over living lives: a reminder of mortality set inside a display of horsemanship.

1840.reading: One man and one elephant looked like a hundred thousand wandering in every direction, and the discerning royal assembly declared there was no one else in the world who could own an elephant, and said no more.
1840.event: The king's assembly proclaims Civakan the one true master of elephants.

1841.reading: When he pressed its striped brow with the tip of his nail, the understanding elephant stood still at once, its two bells rang, and the flood-like crowd shook their hands in wonder.
1841.event: At a touch of his nail the elephant halts and the crowd marvels.
1841.nuance: Line 3's மௌளரும் is not a Tamil word as printed; the bells' sound is clear, the opening word is not.

1842.reading: Some say that the good-minded elephant moved with the prince as if saying 'my mind and yours are not two', like one telling himself what is in his own heart.
1842.nuance: The words of union, my mind and yours not two, are the lovers' and friends' language, here given to a rider and his beast; என்மரும் marks it as one view among those who saw.

links.note: In 454 Civakan turned back the hunters' raid on the king's herd; here his friends plan a raid on a king's herd to make him ride out.
links.teaches: The cattle raid that first made Civakan a public hero becomes a signal his friends can send him, so the epic treats his response to niraikol as a known trait that others can plan on.

links.note: Mastering a king's must elephant brings Civakan the usurper's threat to brand him a thief with the elephant's tusk in 1121, and a lawful king's assembly's acclaim here.
links.teaches: The same feat earns punishment under Kattiyangaran and honour under Tadamittan, so the epic makes the court's response to Civakan's prowess a measure of the ruler, not of the deed.

links.note: With Asanivegam Civakan only dodged between the tusks and drove the beast away; here he mounts, harnesses and pats the must elephant until it obeys gladly.
links.teaches: Set side by side, the two elephant scenes show the hero's mastery grown from escaping a beast to commanding and calming one, the step from youthful daring to the skill a king's court rewards.

links.note: The Kural trusts the concurring word of three spies who do not know one another; the friends' three spies come back together (ஒன்றி) with one report.
links.teaches: The epic keeps the Kural's number three but drops its safeguard of mutual ignorance, showing a band of friends using the statecraft rule loosely, with trust in place of cross-checking.

gains.a: the friends' three spies are seen to follow a recognised rule of intelligence rather than a chance number
gains.b: the couplet's condition that spies not know one another stands out once a story shows three who arrive together

links.note: The Kural says to think before resolving, since rethinking after resolving is a fault; Buddhisenan says that once the raid is made, turning back brings blame, so weigh it first.
links.teaches: Buddhisenan supplies the reason the Kural leaves unstated: in war, the deed once begun shuts off retreat through blame, which is why the thinking must come before the resolve.

gains.a: Buddhisenan's caution gains the standing of a general maxim of deliberate action, not mere timidity
gains.b: the couplet's bare 'lapse' gains a concrete cost, the blame of retreat before a king's army

links.note: The Kural's huge tusked elephant fears the tiger's attack; Civakan comes at the elephant like a lion (1833), but it ends not in fear but in one mind with him.
links.teaches: Against the Kural's picture of the strong beast cowed by a fiercer one, the epic's elephant is won into agreement, so mastery here is shown as concord after force, not fear alone.

gains.a: the epic's claim that rider and beast share one mind gains force against the common image of the elephant ruled by terror
gains.b: the couplet's image of fear as the end of the contest gains a counter-case in which the stronger spirit ends in rapport

links.note: Maduraikanchi lists a must elephant that kills its goad-men, breaks its post and roams, beside horses drilled in circling courses; 1831 and 1839 give the same post-breaking elephant and the same circling drill.
links.teaches: The Sangam city poem sets the rampaging elephant and the drilled circles side by side as separate noises of the capital, while the epic joins them as two stages of one hero's mastery, riot turned into drill.

gains.a: the epic's set piece is seen to draw on a Sangam catalogue of the capital's elephants and horses
gains.b: the catalogue's separate items gain a story in which one man turns the first into the second

source_issues: 1820 and 1821 were printed in eight half-lines and joined into four by the build; word division in the joined lines is doubtful.
1822 line 4 தானையா is doubtful (perhaps தானையார் or தானையால்).
1834 line 1 அப்புதா தையென: word division doubtful.
1840 line 4 ends என்றதெ., probably for என்றதே.
1841 line 3 opens மௌளரும், not a Tamil word as printed (corrupt); line 2 has ஓய்யென where 1833 and 1838 have ஒய்யென.

cast.role: the hero, living under another name at Emamapuram as teacher of the princes
Civakan's friend, leader of the band that comes seeking him
Civakan's friend, called a man of the four Vedas (named புத்திசேன் in 1829)
Civakan's companions, the four friends and their force (நால்வர் in 1822 and 1829)
Padumukan's men, whom he rouses for the raid
the three spies the friends sent ahead to Emamapuram
the king of Emamapuram's elephant, which goes into must
the royal assembly of Emamapuram, which acclaims Civakan
the great crowd watching the taming
